newsitem.title: USA: Alaska governor secures Sakhalin oil pacts.
newsitem.headline: Alaska governor secures Sakhalin oil pacts.

text.p: Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles and a delegation of business and political leaders from the state said Wednesday they secured several agreements with their Sakhalin counterparts to help Alaskans get involved in the impending oil and gas boom on the Russian Far East island.
Knowles, who led the trade delegation on the four-day trip to Sakhalin, said Alaska could become an important service and staging area for oil development for that promising Russian prospect.
"If you want to fly from Seattle to Sakhalin, you'll have to fly right over Anchorage," the Democratic governor said in a news conference held the day after the delegation's return home.
During his time in Sakhalin, Knowles dedicated an American Business Center and arranged several financial, environmental and business agreements.
A partnership plan was signed by a National Bank of Alaska official and Sakhalin counterparts to improve financing of large projects.
Alaska and Sakhalin officials signed a memorandum of understanding on environmental protection to establish rules similar to those in place in Alaska.

And officials signed a memorandum of agreement to continue development through the Alaska-Sakhalin Working Group, a goverment and business panel set up in 1994 to cooperate in finance, taxation, environmental protection, transportation, trade and education.

Alaska House of Representatives Speaker Gail Phillips said the industry situation in Sakhalin is similar to the one that existed in Alaska in the early 1970s, when development was just starting on the giant Prudhoe Bay field and the trans-Alaska pipeline.
Phillips, who accompanied Knowles on the trip, said Sakhalin officials would like to see much of the contracted work go to Alaska companies.
"They have an opportunity to work with anybody in the world," the Republican lawmaker said. "They feel a real kinship with us in Alaska."

Nonetheless, Alaska and U.S. companies have "behind the curve" in participating in the impending Sakhalin oil and gas boom, said Bill Stamps, an Alaska official with Peak Oilfield Service Co. and a member of the trade delegation.
Companies and governments from Japan, Germany, Denmark and elsewhere have been much more aggressive in Sahkalin, Stamps said.
Even other West Coast states have beat Alaska to Sakhalin, he said. "California, Oregon and Washington (state) are all ahead of us, as well, so we're playing catch-up," he said.

However, he said, Alaska companies have several advantages when trying to sell their services on the Russian Far East Island -- geograpic proximity and experience with a similar climate and landscape.
"California, Oregon and Washington don't have permafrost," he said.
